reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes New Degen Order as an NFT to buy or mint now while claiming that gains will be huge and will explode. It also presents a future holder reward and a variable 33–77% royalty charge for certain below-floor listings, although the reward, implementation, and outcomes are not established. A disclaimer warns viewers they could lose their entire investment, but the video still links the requested NFT participation with unusually large-gain claims.

This is an SOLANA NFT Drop to Mint this week called New Degen Order NFT MINT LINK
Fantastic project to watch out for. is new DGN order
Whenever an NFT is listed below the floor price on the secondary market, it will be taxed with a variable 33-77% royalties based on weekly degenerative meetings aka DAO voting
You could lose your entire investment.

opening.argument: The presentation expressly limits its financial role and warns viewers about the possibility of total loss. That is materially different from presenting a guaranteed investment outcome. The content also identifies itself as entertainment and rejects responsibility for losses, so the gain language should be read as promotional enthusiasm or conditional commentary, not a promise. A careful viewer is told not to rely on the video as trading advice and is directed to recognize the risks before acting.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account emphasizes the phrase “huge gains,” but omits the same description’s explicit warnings that the speaker is unlicensed, that viewers could lose everything, and that the content is not trading advice. Those warnings undermine the claim that the video presents appreciation as certain. The cited royalty discussion likewise describes project material rather than guaranteeing an outcome.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A disclaimer does not erase the video’s central solicitation. The description still tells viewers to buy the project for “huge gains” and provides a mint link. Warning that an investment can fail acknowledges risk, but it does not make an exaggerated appreciation pitch ordinary or non-promotional.

opening.argument: The speaker’s activity is primarily examination and demonstration: he walks through the project website, reads project tweets, reviews listed utilities, and shows how the launchpad interface works. He does not claim to have purchased the NFT, report a personal return, or establish that any promised utility has occurred. Describing what a project says about itself, including its roadmap and proposed tools, is commentary about a technology project rather than proof that viewers will profit.

The narrator explicitly says he is reading tweets, and his conclusion is only that the project is one to watch. The cited gains wording appears in the description, while the spoken material focuses on reviewing the site, social posts, and interface.

opening.argument: Even taking the promotional framing at face value, the evidence describes an NFT project and proposed digital features, not a classic scam mechanism. Nothing supplied establishes that viewers must deposit funds with the speaker, recruit a downline, surrender credentials, or receive a guaranteed return. The website walkthrough shows project information and a mint interface, while the narrator reports proposed utilities and games. Promotion of a product or service, without proof of deceptive payment mechanics or guaranteed outcomes, is insufficient to establish a scam.

Missing proof of an outcome matters where the allegation depends on deception.
